# Project Introduction

## Business Problem

Emergency medical services (EMS) must respond to changing demand while maintaining timely emergency response. Fluctuations in incident volume can complicate staffing, ambulance availability, and resource planning. Understanding historical demand patterns and response times may help emergency services better anticipate future needs.

## Project Objectives

The goal of this project is to apply time-series analysis and forecasting methods to NYC emergency medical services data.

The specific objectives are to:

1.  Identify historical trends, seasonal patterns, and unusual changes in weekly EMS demand.

2.  Forecast total weekly EMS incidents and compare demand patterns between life-threatening and non-life-threatening emergencies.

3.  Analyze historical response-time patterns and develop forecasts of weekly average response times.

4.  Evaluate forecasting performance and discuss how the results could support emergency service planning.

## Project Scope

The analysis uses publicly available weekly NYC 911 data from November 2013 through September 2026, focusing on emergency medical services. The project examines incident counts and response-time measurements for life-threatening and non-life-threatening emergencies.

The findings are intended to support operational planning rather than predict individual emergency incidents or individual ambulance arrival times.

# Dataset Description and Initial Exploration

## Data Source and Overview

The dataset used in this project is the **NYC 911 End-to-End Data**, obtained from NYC Open Data.

**Source:** <https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Public-Safety/911-End-to-End-Data/t7p9-n9dy>

The dataset contains weekly emergency incident counts and response-time measurements for several New York City emergency service agencies, including EMS, FDNY, and NYPD.

Our analysis will focus specifically on EMS incidents, including life-threatening and non-life-threatening medical emergencies.

The original dataset will be preserved, and a cleaned version will be prepared for time-series analysis and forecasting.

## Loading Required Libraries

```{r}
# Load packages for data preparation and time-series analysis
library(fpp3)
library(here)
```

## Importing and Inspecting the Raw Dataset

Before cleaning the data, we will examine its structure, dimensions, variable names, and data types to understand what information is available and identify potential data quality issues.

```{r}


# Import the original NYC 911 dataset
ems_raw <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("data", "raw", "911_End-to-End_Data_20261104.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

```

```{r}

# Identify problems encountered when importing the dataset
readr::problems(ems_raw)

```

```{r}

# Identify the variables with parsing problems
names(ems_raw)[c(6, 8)]

```

The initial CSV import identified two parsing issues in a single record, involving numeric values containing thousands separators. The affected variables were Call to PD Calltaker Handoff and Call to FDNY Job Creation. These issues were investigated further in Investigating CSV Parsing Issues subsection, where they were traced to an FDNY record outside the scope of the EMS analysis. Consequently, no corrections to these measurements were necessary for the cleaned EMS dataset.

## Dataset Structure and Description

This section examines the dataset's size, historical coverage, and emergency service categories. Understanding these characteristics will help determine which observations are relevant to our EMS time-series analysis.

```{r}

# Examine dataset dimensions and historical coverage
ems_raw |>
  mutate(
    Week_Check = lubridate::mdy(`Week Start Date`)
  ) |>
  summarise(
    Total_Records = n(),
    Total_Variables = ncol(ems_raw),
    First_Week = min(Week_Check, na.rm = TRUE),
    Last_Week = max(Week_Check, na.rm = TRUE),
    Missing_Dates = sum(is.na(Week_Check))
  )

```

```{r}

# Count records by emergency service agency
ems_raw |>
  count(Agency, name = "Records")

# Examine the EMS incident categories
ems_raw |>
  filter(Agency == "EMS") |>
  count(`Final Incident Type`, name = "Records")

```

The original NYC 911 dataset contains records from four emergency service agency groups: EMS, FDNY, NYPD, and NYPD (Non-CIP). This project focuses specifically on EMS-reported medical emergency demand and call-to-arrival times. Therefore, only records classified under the EMS agency were selected for analysis.

Although FDNY also reports medical emergencies, combining its records with EMS observations could introduce overlapping incident counts and differences in agency-specific reporting practices. NYPD records were excluded because they represent police-related emergency activity rather than the medical emergency demand being forecasted.

This filtering decision maintains a consistent definition of EMS demand throughout the study. The original dataset remains unchanged, and the findings apply specifically to EMS-reported incidents rather than all emergencies handled by New York City's emergency services.

The NYC 911 dataset contains 12,327 records and 30 variables, covering November 18, 2013, through September 21, 2026. All records contain valid dates.

The dataset includes four emergency service agency groups. Our analysis will focus on the 1,364 EMS records, consisting of 671 observations for each of the two primary emergency categories and 22 records with missing incident classifications. These unclassified records will be examined during the data quality assessment.

# Data Quality Assessment

## Missing Incident Classifications

```{r}

# Investigate EMS records with missing incident categories
ems_raw |>
  filter(
    Agency == "EMS",
    is.na(`Final Incident Type`)
  ) |>
  summarise(
    Records = n(),
    Total_Incidents = sum(
      `# of Incidents Calculated`,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    Missing_Incident_Counts = sum(
      is.na(`# of Incidents Calculated`)
    )
  )

```

The EMS dataset contains 22 records with missing emergency classifications, representing 23 incidents. All 22 records have valid incident counts. These incidents will be included when calculating total EMS demand but excluded from comparisons between life-threatening and non-life-threatening emergencies because their classifications are unknown.

## Missing Values in Key EMS Variables

```{r}

# Check missing values in the variables relevant to our project
ems_raw |>
  filter(Agency == "EMS") |>
  summarise(
    Total_Records = n(),
    Missing_Dates = sum(is.na(`Week Start Date`)),
    Missing_Categories = sum(is.na(`Final Incident Type`)),
    Missing_Incidents = sum(is.na(`# of Incidents Calculated`)),
    Missing_Arrival = sum(is.na(`Call to Agency Arrival`)),
    Missing_Dispatch = sum(is.na(`Average Dispatch`)),
    Missing_Travel = sum(is.na(`Average Travel`))
  )

```

The missing-value assessment identified 22 records with missing emergency classifications and one record with a missing average dispatch time. No missing values were found in the dates, incident counts, call-to-arrival times, or average travel times. Overall, the EMS data show a high level of completeness for the variables relevant to our forecasting objectives.

## Investigating the Missing Dispatch Time

```{r}

# Identify the EMS record with a missing dispatch time
ems_raw |>
  filter(
    Agency == "EMS",
    is.na(`Average Dispatch`)
  ) |>
  select(
    `Week Start Date`,
    `Final Incident Type`,
    `# of Incidents Calculated`,
    `Call to Agency Arrival`,
    `Average Dispatch`,
    `Average Travel`
  )

```

The single missing average dispatch time occurred during the week of February 6, 2017. This record represents one EMS incident and also has an unknown emergency classification. The incident will be retained in total EMS demand calculations, while the missing dispatch value will remain unchanged to avoid introducing an unsupported estimate. The record will be excluded from category-specific analyses because its emergency classification is unavailable.

## Checking for Duplicate Records

```{r}

# Check for completely identical EMS records
ems_raw |>
  filter(Agency == "EMS") |>
  summarise(
    Total_Records = n(),
    Exact_Duplicates = sum(duplicated(pick(everything())))
  )

```

The duplicate assessment found no completely identical records among the 1,364 EMS observations. An additional check will examine whether any week and emergency classification combinations occur more than once, which could affect the preparation of the weekly time series.

## Checking Duplicate Week and Category Combinations

```{r}

# Check whether the same week and emergency category appears more than once
ems_raw |>
  filter(Agency == "EMS") |>
  count(
    `Week Start Date`,
    `Final Incident Type`,
    name = "Records"
  ) |>
  filter(Records > 1) |>
  arrange(desc(Records))

```

The assessment found no duplicate combinations of week start date and emergency classification. Combined with the earlier check for identical records, this confirms that no duplicate EMS observations were identified. No duplicate removal is necessary during data cleaning.

## Checking for Missing Weeks

```{r}

# Check for missing weeks in each classified EMS emergency category
ems_raw |>
  filter(
    Agency == "EMS",
    !is.na(`Final Incident Type`)
  ) |>
  mutate(Week = lubridate::mdy(`Week Start Date`)) |>
  as_tsibble(
    key = `Final Incident Type`,
    index = Week
  ) |>
  has_gaps(.full = TRUE)

```

The weekly continuity assessment found no missing weeks in either the life-threatening or non-life-threatening EMS incident series. Both categories contain regularly spaced weekly observations, making the dataset suitable for time-series forecasting without requiring missing-week imputation.

## Investigating Potential Outliers

```{r}

# Summary statistics for weekly incident counts by emergency category
ems_raw |>
  filter(
    Agency == "EMS",
    !is.na(`Final Incident Type`)
  ) |>
  group_by(`Final Incident Type`) |>
  summarise(
    Observations = n(),
    Mean_Incidents = mean(`# of Incidents Calculated`, na.rm = TRUE),
    Median_Incidents = median(`# of Incidents Calculated`, na.rm = TRUE),
    Min_Incidents = min(`# of Incidents Calculated`, na.rm = TRUE),
    Max_Incidents = max(`# of Incidents Calculated`, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

```

The descriptive statistics show that non-life-threatening emergencies have higher weekly incident counts than life-threatening emergencies, averaging approximately 12,398 and 9,511 incidents, respectively. The means and medians are relatively close for both categories, although their minimum and maximum values indicate substantial variation across weeks. These extreme observations will be investigated further to determine whether they reflect genuine changes in emergency demand or potential data quality issues.

```{r}

# Visualize weekly EMS incidents by emergency category
ems_raw |>
  filter(
    Agency == "EMS",
    !is.na(`Final Incident Type`)
  ) |>
  mutate(Week = lubridate::mdy(`Week Start Date`)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Week, y = `# of Incidents Calculated`)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ `Final Incident Type`, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Weekly NYC EMS Incidents by Emergency Category",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Number of Incidents"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

The time-series plots reveal several notable changes in weekly EMS demand. Life-threatening emergencies increased during the early years of the dataset, followed by relatively stable demand before a pronounced spike around 2020. Non-life-threatening incidents also show an increase in earlier years and a substantial disruption around 2020. These changes coincide with the COVID-19 pandemic, although additional evidence would be needed to establish the causes. Both categories show an unusual decline near the end of the dataset, raising the possibility of incomplete reporting. These observations will be investigated before determining whether any records should be excluded from the forecasting dataset.

```{r}

# Examine recent EMS incident counts for possible incomplete reporting
ems_raw |>
  filter(
    Agency == "EMS",
    !is.na(`Final Incident Type`)
  ) |>
  mutate(Week = lubridate::mdy(`Week Start Date`)) |>
  group_by(`Final Incident Type`) |>
  slice_max(order_by = Week, n = 5) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(
    Week,
    `Final Incident Type`,
    `# of Incidents Calculated`
  ) |>
  arrange(`Final Incident Type`, Week)

```

The final reporting week, September 21, 2026, shows an unusually large decline in EMS incidents compared with the preceding week. Life-threatening incidents decreased by approximately 22.2%, while non-life-threatening incidents decreased by 15.1%, resulting in an overall decline of approximately 18.5%. Because both categories declined simultaneously during the final available week, the observation may reflect incomplete reporting. The final week will be provisionally excluded from the forecasting dataset to reduce the risk of modeling incomplete data. This exclusion is based on a data-quality concern rather than confirmed evidence of incomplete reporting.

```{r}

# Examine the distribution of weekly EMS incident counts
ems_raw |>
  filter(
    Agency == "EMS",
    !is.na(`Final Incident Type`)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = `Final Incident Type`,
    y = `# of Incidents Calculated`
  )) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c(
    "1. Life Threating Med Emergencies" = "Life-Threatening",
    "2. Non-Life Threatening Med Emergencies" = "Non-Life-Threatening"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Weekly NYC EMS Incidents",
    x = "Emergency Category",
    y = "Weekly Incidents"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()


```

The boxplots show that non-life-threatening EMS incidents generally have higher weekly counts than life-threatening incidents, with median values of approximately 12,560 and 9,713 incidents, respectively. Both categories contain observations outside the typical range, including unusually high and low weekly counts. These observations may represent genuine changes in emergency demand rather than data errors. Therefore, outliers will not be automatically removed, although the potentially incomplete final reporting week will be handled separately.

## Examining EMS Response Times

```{r}

# Visualize weekly average EMS call-to-arrival times
ems_raw |>
  filter(
    Agency == "EMS",
    !is.na(`Final Incident Type`)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Week = lubridate::mdy(`Week Start Date`),
    Arrival_Minutes = `Call to Agency Arrival` / 60
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Week, y = Arrival_Minutes)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ `Final Incident Type`, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Weekly NYC EMS Call-to-Arrival Times",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Average Call-to-Arrival Time (Minutes)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

The response-time analysis reveals substantial differences between life-threatening and non-life-threatening EMS emergencies. Life-threatening emergencies generally have shorter call-to-arrival times, while non-life-threatening emergencies experience longer and more variable response times. Both categories show an upward trend in recent years, with particularly pronounced increases in non-life-threatening response times during 2025–2026. The series also contain several extreme spikes, including observations around 2020. Notably, response times have increased during periods when incident counts appear relatively stable, suggesting that factors beyond demand volume may influence EMS response performance. These findings warrant further investigation before forecasting and should not be interpreted as evidence of specific operational causes.

```{r}

# Identify the five highest call-to-arrival times in each EMS category
ems_raw |>
  filter(
    Agency == "EMS",
    !is.na(`Final Incident Type`)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Week = lubridate::mdy(`Week Start Date`),
    Arrival_Minutes = `Call to Agency Arrival` / 60
  ) |>
  group_by(`Final Incident Type`) |>
  slice_max(order_by = Arrival_Minutes, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(
    Week,
    `Final Incident Type`,
    `# of Incidents Calculated`,
    Arrival_Minutes
  ) |>
  arrange(`Final Incident Type`, desc(Arrival_Minutes))

```

The investigation of extreme call-to-arrival times identified March 23, 2020, as the week with the highest average response time in both emergency categories, coinciding with unusually high incident volumes. However, several other extreme observations occurred during 2025–2026, even when weekly incident counts were closer to their typical levels. In particular, non-life-threatening emergencies experienced average call-to-arrival times exceeding 40 minutes in several recent weeks. These findings suggest that emergency demand alone may not explain the observed increases in response times. Because the extreme observations may represent genuine operational conditions, they will be retained unless further investigation identifies measurement errors.

## Checking for Invalid Numerical Values

```{r}

# Check for zero or negative values in key EMS measurements
ems_raw |>
  filter(Agency == "EMS") |>
  summarise(
    Negative_Incidents = sum(`# of Incidents Calculated` < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    Zero_Incidents = sum(`# of Incidents Calculated` == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    Negative_Arrival = sum(`Call to Agency Arrival` < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    Zero_Arrival = sum(`Call to Agency Arrival` == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    Negative_Dispatch = sum(`Average Dispatch` < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    Negative_Travel = sum(`Average Travel` < 0, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

```

The numerical validation identified no negative or zero incident counts and no negative or zero call-to-arrival times. Additionally, no negative dispatch or travel times were detected. These findings indicate that the key EMS measurements do not contain obvious invalid values based on the conditions tested. The previously identified missing dispatch-time observation remains documented separately. Although these results support the overall quality of the dataset, they do not rule out all possible measurement or reporting errors

## Investigating CSV Parsing Issues

```{r}

# Identify parsing issues detected during CSV import
readr::problems(ems_raw)

```

```{r}

# Identify the variables and agency affected by the parsing warnings
names(ems_raw)[c(6, 8)]

ems_raw |>
  slice(4944) |>
  select(
    `Week Start Date`,
    Agency,
    `Final Incident Type`
  )

```

The CSV import generated two parsing warnings involving numeric values containing thousands separators. Both warnings occurred in the same source record, affecting columns 6 and 8. These values may have been incorrectly imported as missing because of their formatting. The affected variables and agency will be examined before determining whether corrective action is necessary for the EMS analysis.

```{r}

# Verify which EMS observation contains the parsing errors
ems_raw |>
  slice(4943:4944) |>
  select(
    `Week Start Date`,
    Agency,
    `Final Incident Type`,
    `Call to PD Calltaker Handoff`,
    `Call to FDNY Job Creation`,
    `# of Incidents Calculated`,
    `Call to Agency Arrival`
  )

```

The CSV import produced two parsing warnings involving values containing thousands separators. Further investigation located both errors in an FDNY record dated August 2, 2021, affecting the Call to PD Calltaker Handoff and Call to FDNY Job Creation variables. The corresponding EMS record retained valid incident-count and call-to-arrival measurements. Because the parsing issues occur outside the EMS records used for this project, no correction is necessary for the primary forecasting analysis. The original CSV will remain unchanged.

## Data Quality Assessment Summary

The data-quality assessment indicates that the NYC EMS dataset is generally suitable for time-series analysis. Both classified emergency categories contain complete weekly observations, with no duplicate records or invalid incident counts identified. A small number of records have missing emergency classifications, while one unclassified record also has a missing dispatch time. Several extreme incident counts and response times were identified but will be retained because they may reflect genuine emergency conditions. Two CSV parsing warnings were traced to an FDNY record and do not affect the primary EMS forecasting variables. The final reporting week remains a potential data-quality concern and will be provisionally excluded from the forecasting dataset. These findings will guide the data-cleaning and preparation procedures in the following section.

```{r}

# Verify the observation period for each EMS emergency category
ems_raw |>
  filter(
    Agency == "EMS",
    !is.na(`Final Incident Type`)
  ) |>
  mutate(Week = lubridate::mdy(`Week Start Date`)) |>
  group_by(`Final Incident Type`) |>
  summarise(
    First_Week = min(Week),
    Last_Week = max(Week),
    Total_Weeks = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

```

The final date validation confirmed that both EMS emergency categories contain 671 consecutive weekly observations, covering November 18, 2013, through September 21, 2026. Both series have identical starting and ending dates, with no missing weeks. This alignment supports consistent comparisons between life-threatening and non-life-threatening incidents and allows the categories to be combined for total weekly EMS demand analysis.

# Data Cleaning and Preparation

## Filtering and Standardizing EMS Records

The data preparation process focuses on creating a consistent weekly EMS dataset for forecasting incident demand and analyzing response times. The original NYC 911 dataset will remain unchanged, while the processed data will include only EMS observations and variables relevant to the project. Emergency classifications, dates, and measurement names will be standardized to improve readability and reproducibility. Potentially incomplete reporting periods and unclassified incidents will be handled using the findings from the data-quality assessment.

```{r}

# Filter EMS observations and standardize key variables
ems_data <- ems_raw |>
  filter(Agency == "EMS") |>
  transmute(
    Week = lubridate::mdy(`Week Start Date`),
    Category = case_when(
      `Final Incident Type` == "1. Life Threating Med Emergencies" ~ "Life-Threatening",
      `Final Incident Type` == "2. Non-Life Threatening Med Emergencies" ~ "Non-Life-Threatening",
      TRUE ~ "Unclassified"
    ),
    Incidents = `# of Incidents Calculated`,
    Arrival_Seconds = `Call to Agency Arrival`,
    Dispatch_Minutes = `Average Dispatch`,
    Travel_Minutes = `Average Travel`
    

  )

# Verify the prepared dataset
ems_data |>
  count(Category, name = "Records")

```

The EMS filtering and standardization process retained 1,364 observations, including 671 life-threatening, 671 non-life-threatening, and 22 unclassified records. The original emergency classifications were replaced with standardized category labels, and the relevant incident-count and response-time variables were renamed for clarity. No records were removed during this step.

## Handling the Potentially Incomplete Final Week

```{r}

# Exclude the potentially incomplete final reporting week
ems_clean <- ems_data |>
  filter(Week < as.Date("2026-09-21"))

# Verify the remaining records and date range
ems_clean |>
  summarise(
    Total_Records = n(),
    First_Week = min(Week),
    Last_Week = max(Week)
  )

# Confirm the number of records in each category
ems_clean |>
  count(Category, name = "Records")

```

The September 21, 2026, reporting week was provisionally excluded because of a substantial and simultaneous decline in both EMS emergency categories, raising concerns about reporting completeness. This removed two observations and reduced the prepared dataset from 1,364 to 1,362 records. Both classified categories now contain 670 weekly observations, covering November 18, 2013, through September 14, 2026. All 22 unclassified records were retained. The exclusion remains a documented assumption rather than a confirmed reporting error.

## Preparing Classified and Unclassified EMS Records

```{r}

# Prepare records with known emergency classifications
ems_classified <- ems_clean |>
  filter(Category != "Unclassified")

# Keep unclassified records separately for total demand calculations
ems_unclassified <- ems_clean |>
  filter(Category == "Unclassified")

# Verify the records and incident counts
tibble(
  Dataset = c("Classified", "Unclassified"),
  Records = c(nrow(ems_classified), nrow(ems_unclassified)),
  Total_Incidents = c(
    sum(ems_classified$Incidents),
    sum(ems_unclassified$Incidents)
  )
)

```

The prepared EMS data were separated into classified and unclassified observations. The classified dataset contains 1,340 records representing 14,682,715 incidents, while the 22 unclassified records represent an additional 23 incidents. Together, these datasets account for 14,682,738 incidents across the retained reporting period. Unclassified incidents will be included in total EMS demand calculations but excluded from category-specific analyses, preserving valid incident counts without assigning unsupported emergency classifications.

## Creating the Weekly EMS Demand Dataset

```{r}

# Aggregate all EMS incidents into one total per week
ems_weekly_total <- ems_clean |>
  group_by(Week) |>
  summarise(
    Total_Incidents = sum(Incidents),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(Week)

# Verify the total weekly dataset
ems_weekly_total |>
  summarise(
    Total_Weeks = n(),
    First_Week = min(Week),
    Last_Week = max(Week),
    Total_Incidents = sum(Total_Incidents)
  )

```

The weekly EMS demand dataset was created by aggregating incident counts across all emergency classifications, including unclassified observations. The resulting dataset contains 670 weekly observations from November 18, 2013, through September 14, 2026, representing 14,682,738 incidents. The aggregate incident count matches the total calculated during data preparation, confirming that no incidents were lost during aggregation. This dataset provides a consistent weekly series for forecasting overall EMS demand.

## Preparing the Category-Level EMS Dataset

```{r}


# Prepare weekly EMS data for each emergency category
ems_weekly_category <- ems_classified |>
  select(
    Week,
    Category,
    Incidents,
    Arrival_Seconds,
    Dispatch_Minutes,
    Travel_Minutes
  ) |>
  arrange(Category, Week)

# Verify the number of observations in each category
ems_weekly_category |>
  group_by(Category) |>
  summarise(
    Total_Weeks = n(),
    First_Week = min(Week),
    Last_Week = max(Week),
    Missing_Incidents = sum(is.na(Incidents)),
    Missing_Arrival = sum(is.na(Arrival_Seconds)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


```

The category-level EMS dataset contains 1,340 observations, with 670 weekly records for each emergency classification. Both categories cover November 18, 2013, through September 14, 2026, and contain no missing incident counts or call-to-arrival measurements. The original weekly response-time values were preserved without additional aggregation, ensuring that the dataset remains suitable for category-specific demand forecasting and response-time analysis.

## Validating the Prepared Datasets

```{r}

# Compare total weekly incidents with the sum of classified incidents
weekly_check <- ems_weekly_category |>
  group_by(Week) |>
  summarise(
    Classified_Incidents = sum(Incidents),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  left_join(ems_weekly_total, by = "Week") |>
  mutate(
    Difference = Total_Incidents - Classified_Incidents
  )

# Summarize differences between the datasets
weekly_check |>
  summarise(
    Total_Weeks = n(),
    Weeks_With_Differences = sum(Difference != 0),
    Total_Difference = sum(Difference),
    Negative_Differences = sum(Difference < 0),
    Missing_Differences = sum(is.na(Difference))
  )

```

The consistency assessment confirmed that the total and category-level EMS datasets agree across all 670 reporting weeks. Differences were identified in 22 weeks, representing 23 incidents without emergency classifications. This matches the previously documented unclassified records. No negative or missing differences were identified, indicating that the weekly aggregation preserved incident counts and correctly incorporated unclassified incidents into total EMS demand.

## Final Structural Validation

```{r}

# Validate the final weekly datasets
tibble(
  Dataset = c("Total EMS", "EMS by Category"),
  Records = c(nrow(ems_weekly_total), nrow(ems_weekly_category)),
  Duplicate_Keys = c(
    sum(duplicated(ems_weekly_total$Week)),
    sum(duplicated(ems_weekly_category[c("Week", "Category")]))
  ),
  Missing_Incidents = c(
    sum(is.na(ems_weekly_total$Total_Incidents)),
    sum(is.na(ems_weekly_category$Incidents))
  ),
  Missing_Dates = c(
    sum(is.na(ems_weekly_total$Week)),
    sum(is.na(ems_weekly_category$Week))
  )
)

```

The final structural validation confirmed that the total EMS dataset contains 670 weekly observations, while the category-level dataset contains 1,340 observations. Neither dataset contains duplicate time-series identifiers, missing dates, or missing incident counts. These results indicate that the data preparation process preserved the expected dataset structure and did not introduce missing values or duplicate observations.

```{r}

# Verify weekly continuity in both prepared datasets
ems_total_ts <- ems_weekly_total |>
  as_tsibble(index = Week)

ems_category_ts <- ems_weekly_category |>
  as_tsibble(key = Category, index = Week)

# Check for missing weeks
has_gaps(ems_total_ts, .full = TRUE)

has_gaps(ems_category_ts, .full = TRUE)

```

The final time-series continuity assessment confirmed that both processed datasets contain regularly spaced weekly observations without missing weeks. The total EMS demand series and both emergency-category series cover the same 670-week reporting period. Combined with the structural and incident-count validation results, these findings confirm that the processed datasets are suitable for subsequent time-series exploratory analysis and forecasting.

## Exporting the Processed Dataset

```{r}


# Combine category-level measurements with total weekly EMS demand
ems_weekly_clean <- ems_weekly_category |>
  left_join(
    ems_weekly_total,
    by = "Week"
  ) |>
  arrange(Week, Category)

# Verify the master dataset
ems_weekly_clean |>
  summarise(
    Records = n(),
    Total_Weeks = n_distinct(Week),
    Missing_Totals = sum(is.na(Total_Incidents))
  )


```

The master cleaned EMS dataset contains 1,340 observations across 670 reporting weeks, with one record per week for each classified emergency category. Total weekly EMS demand was successfully joined to the category-level observations, with no missing weekly totals. The total demand measurements include incidents with unknown classifications, while the category-level measurements preserve the original incident counts and response times. This structure supports the team's forecasting and response-time analyses using a single shared dataset.

```{r}


# Export the master cleaned EMS dataset
readr::write_csv(
  ems_weekly_clean,
  here::here("data", "processed", "ems_weekly_clean.csv")
)

# Verify the exported file exists
file.exists(
  here::here("data", "processed", "ems_weekly_clean.csv")
)


```

# Time-Series Exploratory Data Analysis

## Preparing the Cleaned Data for Time-Series Analysis

Following data cleaning and validation, the prepared EMS dataset will be examined for trends, seasonal patterns, and changes over time. These characteristics are important for understanding emergency demand and selecting appropriate forecasting methods. The analysis will consider both overall EMS demand and the differences between life-threatening and non-life-threatening emergencies.

```{r}

# Examine the prepared time-series datasets
glimpse(ems_total_ts)

glimpse(ems_category_ts)

```

The cleaned EMS data were successfully organized into weekly time-series structures using the `tsibble` framework. The total demand series contains 670 observations, while the category-level dataset contains 1,340 observations across two emergency classifications. Each series uses the reporting week as its time index, and the category-level data preserve incident counts and response-time measurements. These structures support time-series visualization, decomposition, and forecasting using the `fpp3` framework.

## Exploring Trends in Total Weekly EMS Demand

```{r}

# Visualize total weekly EMS demand and its long-term trend
ems_total_ts |>
  autoplot(Total_Incidents) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "red",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Weekly NYC EMS Incidents and Long-Term Trend",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Number of EMS Incidents"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

The total weekly EMS demand series shows substantial changes over the study period. Incident volumes increased from approximately 16,000–18,000 per week in the earlier years to around 23,000–24,000 by 2017–2018. A pronounced spike and subsequent decline occurred around early 2020, coinciding with the COVID-19 pandemic. Demand subsequently recovered, with weekly incident counts generally stabilizing around 22,000–23,000 during more recent years. The LOESS-smoothed trend highlights these broader changes while reducing short-term fluctuations. Overall, the series exhibits a changing trend and major historical disruptions, suggesting that forecasting models should be evaluated carefully rather than assuming a constant growth pattern throughout the entire period.

## Investigating Annual Seasonality in EMS Demand

```{r}

# Examine annual seasonal patterns in total weekly EMS demand
ems_total_ts |>
  gg_season(Total_Incidents, period = "year") +
  labs(
    title = "Annual Seasonal Patterns in NYC EMS Demand",
    x = "Week of Year",
    y = "Weekly EMS Incidents"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

The annual seasonal plot reveals considerable variation in weekly EMS demand across calendar years. Some years show modest increases during late spring or summer, but the timing and magnitude of these changes are not consistent throughout the study period. A pronounced spike around March–April 2020 reflects an unusual disruption that differs substantially from typical yearly patterns. The plot also shows differences in overall incident levels between years, consistent with the changing long-term trend identified earlier. These findings suggest that annual seasonality may be present but is not visually dominant. Further analysis using STL decomposition is needed to distinguish recurring seasonal variation from longer-term changes and irregular events.

## STL Decomposition of Total EMS Demand

```{r}

# Decompose total weekly EMS demand into trend, seasonal, and remainder components
ems_stl <- ems_total_ts |>
  model(
    STL(
      Total_Incidents ~ season(period = 52),
      robust = TRUE
    )
  )

# Plot the STL decomposition
ems_stl |>
  components() |>
  autoplot() +
  labs(
    title = "STL Decomposition of Weekly NYC EMS Demand"
  )

```

The robust STL decomposition separated total weekly EMS demand into trend, seasonal, and remainder components. The trend shows substantial growth during the early study period, followed by a decline around 2020–2021 and a subsequent recovery to relatively stable demand in recent years. The seasonal component reveals recurring annual fluctuations of approximately 1,000 incidents above or below the underlying trend, indicating that seasonal patterns are present. The remainder contains a particularly large positive spike around early 2020, reflecting an unusual increase in demand not explained by the estimated trend or seasonality. Overall, the decomposition suggests that both changing trends and annual seasonal variation may be relevant to forecasting EMS demand, although their predictive usefulness must be evaluated using training and testing data.

## Measuring the Strength of Trend and Seasonality

```{r}

# Measure trend and seasonal strength from the STL components
ems_stl_strength <- ems_stl |>
  components() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  summarise(
    Trend_Strength = max(
      0,
      1 - var(remainder) / var(trend + remainder)
    ),
    Seasonal_Strength = max(
      0,
      1 - var(remainder) / var(season_52 + remainder)
    )
  )

# Display the results
ems_stl_strength

```

The STL-based strength measures indicate a moderately strong trend component (0.658) and weak annual seasonality (0.082) in total weekly EMS demand. The trend strength is consistent with the substantial long-term changes observed throughout the study period, including early growth, the disruption around 2020, and subsequent recovery. Although recurring seasonal fluctuations are visible in the STL decomposition, their strength is limited relative to the remaining variation. These results suggest that changes in the underlying demand level may be more influential than annual seasonality. However, seasonal forecasting approaches should still be evaluated because weak historical seasonal strength does not necessarily imply that seasonal models will perform poorly.

## Comparing Trend and Seasonality by Emergency Category

To determine whether seasonal and trend characteristics differ by emergency classification, separate STL decompositions will be performed for life-threatening and non-life-threatening EMS incidents. The resulting trend and seasonal strength measures will be compared to identify differences that may be relevant to category-specific forecasting.

```{r}


# Fit STL decompositions for each emergency category
ems_category_stl <- ems_category_ts |>
  model(
    STL(
      Incidents ~ season(period = 52),
      robust = TRUE
    )
  )

# Plot the original overlaid STL decomposition
ems_category_stl |>
  components() |>
  autoplot() +
  scale_color_discrete(
    labels = c(
      "Life-Threatening",
      "Non-Life-Threatening"
    ),
    name = "Emergency Category"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "STL Decomposition of NYC EMS Demand by Emergency Category",
    x = "Week"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_blank(),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 10)
  ) +
  guides(
    color = guide_legend(nrow = 1)
  )

```

The category-specific STL decompositions reveal differences in the behavior of life-threatening and non-life-threatening EMS incidents. Non-life-threatening emergencies consistently account for higher weekly incident volumes and generally exhibit larger seasonal fluctuations in absolute terms. Both series experienced pronounced disruptions around 2020, followed by periods of recovery. More recently, life-threatening demand has remained relatively stable, while non-life-threatening demand shows a modest decline. The seasonal components indicate recurring annual patterns in both categories, although their relative strengths require further measurement. Large remainder fluctuations around 2020 suggest that unusual events influenced both emergency categories beyond their estimated trends and seasonal patterns.

```{r}

# Measure trend and seasonal strength for each EMS category
ems_category_strength <- ems_category_stl |>
  components() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(Category) |>
  summarise(
    Trend_Strength = max(
      0,
      1 - var(remainder) / var(trend + remainder)
    ),
    Seasonal_Strength = max(
      0,
      1 - var(remainder) / var(season_52 + remainder)
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Display the category-specific strengths
ems_category_strength

```

The category-specific STL analysis identified moderately strong trend components for both life-threatening (0.642) and non-life-threatening (0.631) EMS incidents. Annual seasonal strength was weak in both categories, measuring 0.079 and 0.076, respectively. These results closely resemble the findings for total EMS demand, suggesting that neither category exhibits strong annual seasonality across the full historical period. However, preliminary analysis of the more recent 2022–2026 period suggested stronger seasonal patterns. This difference indicates that seasonal characteristics may vary across historical periods, particularly when major disruptions are included. A consistent recent-period comparison is therefore warranted before drawing conclusions about the relevance of seasonality for forecasting.

## Comparing Seasonality Across Historical Periods

```{r}

# Calculate recent-period STL decompositions for all three demand series
ems_total_recent_stl <- ems_total_ts |>
  filter(Week >= as.Date("2022-01-03")) |>
  model(
    STL(Total_Incidents ~ season(period = 52), robust = TRUE)
  )

ems_category_recent_stl <- ems_category_ts |>
  filter(Week >= as.Date("2022-01-03")) |>
  model(
    STL(Incidents ~ season(period = 52), robust = TRUE)
  )

# Compare trend and seasonal strength for the recent period
recent_total_strength <- ems_total_recent_stl |>
  components() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  summarise(
    Category = "Total EMS",
    Trend_Strength = max(0, 1 - var(remainder) / var(trend + remainder)),
    Seasonal_Strength = max(0, 1 - var(remainder) / var(season_52 + remainder))
  )

recent_category_strength <- ems_category_recent_stl |>
  components() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(Category) |>
  summarise(
    Trend_Strength = max(0, 1 - var(remainder) / var(trend + remainder)),
    Seasonal_Strength = max(0, 1 - var(remainder) / var(season_52 + remainder)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Display the recent-period results
bind_rows(recent_total_strength, recent_category_strength)

```

```{r}



# Combine full-period and recent-period seasonal strength results
seasonality_comparison <- bind_rows(
  ems_stl_strength |>
    mutate(Category = "Total EMS", Period = "2013–2026"),
  ems_category_strength |>
    mutate(Period = "2013–2026"),
  recent_total_strength |>
    mutate(Period = "2022–2026"),
  recent_category_strength |>
    mutate(Period = "2022–2026")
) |>
  mutate(
    Category = factor(
      Category,
      levels = c(
        "Total EMS",
        "Life-Threatening",
        "Non-Life-Threatening"
      )
    )
  )

# Create a grouped bar chart comparing seasonal strength
ggplot(
  seasonality_comparison,
  aes(x = Category, y = Seasonal_Strength, fill = Period)
) +
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    width = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = round(Seasonal_Strength, 3)),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 0.6),
    breaks = seq(0, 0.6, 0.1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Annual Seasonal Strength of NYC EMS Demand",
    subtitle = "Full Historical Period vs. Recent Period",
    x = "Emergency Category",
    y = "Seasonal Strength (0–1)",
    fill = "Period"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10)
  )

```

A comparison of full-period and recent-period STL decompositions revealed substantial differences in estimated annual seasonal strength. Across the full 2013–2026 period, seasonal strength was weak for total EMS demand (0.082), life-threatening incidents (0.079), and non-life-threatening incidents (0.076). However, during the more recent 2022–2026 period, seasonal strength increased to 0.470, 0.432, and 0.407, respectively, indicating more distinguishable annual patterns. Recent-period trend strength was highest for non-life-threatening emergencies (0.514), compared with total EMS demand (0.346) and life-threatening emergencies (0.295). These findings suggest that the characteristics of EMS demand differ across historical periods. The results support evaluating seasonal forecasting approaches and considering alternative training windows, while recognizing that model performance must ultimately be assessed using held-out observations.

## Examining the Relationship Between EMS Demand and Response Times

```{r}

# Examine the relationship between weekly incidents and call-to-arrival times
ems_category_ts |>
  mutate(
    Arrival_Minutes = Arrival_Seconds / 60
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Incidents, y = Arrival_Minutes)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "red"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ Category, scales = "free") +
  labs(
    title = "EMS Incident Demand and Call-to-Arrival Times",
    x = "Weekly EMS Incidents",
    y = "Average Call-to-Arrival Time (Minutes)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

The scatterplots reveal different relationships between weekly incident demand and average call-to-arrival times across EMS emergency classifications. Life-threatening emergencies exhibit a positive linear association, suggesting that higher weekly incident volumes tend to coincide with longer response times. In contrast, non-life-threatening emergencies show a nearly flat regression trend, indicating little apparent overall linear association between demand and response time. Considerable variation remains in both categories, particularly for non-life-threatening emergencies, where some weeks experience substantially longer arrival times despite typical incident volumes. These findings suggest that incident demand alone may not adequately explain response-time variation. The observed associations are descriptive and should not be interpreted as causal relationships.

```{r}

# Calculate correlation between weekly EMS incidents and arrival times
ems_category_ts |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(Category) |>
  summarise(
    Correlation = cor(
      Incidents,
      Arrival_Seconds,
      use = "complete.obs"
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

```

Pearson correlation analysis identified a moderate positive association between weekly incident counts and average call-to-arrival times for life-threatening emergencies (r = 0.454). In contrast, non-life-threatening emergencies showed almost no overall linear association (r = 0.018). These results indicate that the relationship between EMS demand and response times differs by emergency classification. While higher life-threatening incident volumes tend to coincide with longer arrival times, non-life-threatening response times exhibit substantial variation that is not closely associated with weekly demand across the full study period. These correlations are descriptive and do not establish causation, particularly because long-term trends and historical disruptions may influence both variables.

## Comparing Demand–Response Relationships Across Historical Periods

```{r}

# Compare demand and response-time correlations across historical periods
ems_category_ts |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(Category) |>
  summarise(
    Full_Period_Correlation = cor(
      Incidents,
      Arrival_Seconds,
      use = "complete.obs"
    ),
    Recent_Period_Correlation = cor(
      Incidents[Week >= as.Date("2022-01-03")],
      Arrival_Seconds[Week >= as.Date("2022-01-03")],
      use = "complete.obs"
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


```

Comparing correlations across historical periods revealed changes in the relationship between EMS incident demand and call-to-arrival times. For life-threatening emergencies, the correlation decreased from 0.454 across the full 2013–2026 period to 0.350 during 2022–2026, indicating a weaker but still positive recent association. For non-life-threatening emergencies, the correlation changed from approximately zero (0.018) across the full period to a negative association (−0.310) in the recent period. This difference may partly reflect opposing trends in incident volumes and arrival times rather than a direct effect of demand on response performance. Overall, the findings indicate that demand–response relationships vary by emergency category and historical period. Further forecasting analysis should account for these temporal patterns and avoid interpreting correlations as causal effects.

## Summary of EDA Findings and Implications for Forecasting

| Finding | Evidence | Implication for forecasting |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Changing long-term demand | Growth before 2020, followed by disruption and recovery | Models should account for changes in demand over time |
| Stronger recent seasonality | Recent seasonal strength: 0.407–0.470, compared with approximately 0.08 historically | Evaluate seasonal and nonseasonal forecasting models |
| Major historical disruptions | Large incident-count spikes and declines around 2020 | Consider how unusual events affect model performance |
| Different emergency categories | Life-threatening and non-life-threatening incidents have different demand trends | Category-specific forecasting may provide additional insights |
| Increasing arrival times | Particularly pronounced for non-life-threatening incidents during 2025–2026 | Response times should be analyzed separately from incident demand |
| Changing demand–response relationships | Recent correlations: +0.350 for life-threatening and −0.310 for non-life-threatening incidents | Incident volume alone may not adequately explain response times |

The exploratory time-series analysis identified changing long-term trends, recurring annual seasonality, and substantial historical disruptions in NYC EMS demand. Seasonal patterns were more distinguishable during the recent 2022–2026 period than across the full historical dataset, suggesting that the choice of training period may influence forecasting results. Differences between life-threatening and non-life-threatening emergencies were also observed in both demand patterns and response times. In particular, recent increases in call-to-arrival times were not consistently accompanied by increases in incident volumes. These findings support evaluating multiple forecasting approaches, comparing performance on chronological testing data, and analyzing emergency categories separately when appropriate. The exploratory results provide a foundation for subsequent demand and response-time modeling but do not establish causal relationships.

# Reproducibility and Team Handoff

## Verifying the Exported Dataset

```{r}

# Reimport the exported dataset independently
ems_export_check <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("data", "processed", "ems_weekly_clean.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Verify the exported dataset matches the prepared data
tibble(
  Check = c(
    "Number of records",
    "Number of weeks",
    "Total missing values",
    "Export matches prepared data"
  ),
  Result = c(
    as.character(nrow(ems_export_check)),
    as.character(n_distinct(ems_export_check$Week)),
    as.character(sum(is.na(ems_export_check))),
    as.character(isTRUE(all.equal(
      as_tibble(ems_weekly_clean),
      as_tibble(ems_export_check)
    )))
  )
)

```

The exported master EMS dataset was independently reimported and compared with the prepared dataset. Validation confirmed that the CSV contains 1,340 observations across 670 reporting weeks, with no missing values. The reimported data also matched the prepared dataset, confirming that the export process preserved its contents. These findings support the reproducibility of the dataset and its use in subsequent forecasting analyses.

## Master Dataset Description and Data Dictionary

The final master dataset, `ems_weekly_clean.csv`, contains seven variables used to analyze weekly EMS incident demand and response times. Each observation represents one emergency classification during a particular reporting week. The variables were standardized to improve readability and facilitate reproducible analysis.

| Variable | Description | Unit |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| `Week` | Starting date of the reporting week | Date |
| `Category` | Classification as life-threatening or non-life-threatening | Categorical |
| `Incidents` | Number of EMS incidents in the specified category during the week | Incidents |
| `Arrival_Seconds` | Average time between the 911 call entering the system and an emergency unit arriving on scene | Seconds |
| `Dispatch_Minutes` | Average time between job creation and unit assignment | Minutes |
| `Travel_Minutes` | Average time between unit assignment and arrival on scene | Minutes |
| `Total_Incidents` | Total EMS incidents during the week, including incidents with unknown classifications | Incidents |

The dataset contains two records per week, one for each classified emergency category. Consequently, `Total_Incidents` is repeated twice for every week. When analyzing overall EMS demand, only one weekly total should be used to prevent double-counting.

The dataset covers November 18, 2013, through September 14, 2026, following the provisional exclusion of the final reporting week due to potential incomplete reporting.

```{r}
# Extract total EMS demand without double-counting
ems_total <- ems_export_check |>
  distinct(Week, Total_Incidents) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Week)

# Prepare separate emergency-category time series
ems_categories <- ems_export_check |>
  as_tsibble(key = Category, index = Week)
```

## Data Cleaning Decisions and Limitations

The data preparation process followed several documented decisions to preserve valid observations while addressing potential data-quality concerns.

- **Agency selection:** Only EMS records were retained because the project focuses on emergency medical services.

- **Missing classifications:** Twenty-two records representing 23 incidents had unknown emergency classifications. These incidents were included in total weekly demand but excluded from category-specific analyses.

- **Missing measurements:** One unclassified observation contained a missing dispatch-time value. No replacement value was introduced.

- **Duplicate records:** No exact duplicates or duplicate week-category combinations were identified.

- **Extreme observations:** Unusual incident counts and call-to-arrival times were retained because they may reflect genuine emergency conditions.

- **CSV parsing warnings:** Two parsing issues were traced to an FDNY record outside the EMS analysis.

- **Final reporting week:** September 21, 2026, was provisionally excluded because of an unusual decline in both emergency categories. Reporting incompleteness has not been independently confirmed.

The resulting master dataset preserves the weekly incident counts and response-time measurements for both classified emergency categories. Total weekly demand includes unclassified incidents and is repeated across category rows, requiring users to select one total per week when forecasting overall demand. The original CSV remains unchanged to support reproducibility.

## Technical Notes for Forecasting

The cleaned master dataset, `ems_weekly_clean.csv`, contains 670 consecutive weeks of EMS observations from November 18, 2013, through September 14, 2026.

The following considerations should guide subsequent modeling:

- **Total EMS demand:** The `Total_Incidents` column appears twice per week because the dataset contains two classified emergency categories. Extract one total per week to avoid double-counting.

- **Emergency categories:** Use `Category` to distinguish life-threatening and non-life-threatening emergencies when developing category-specific models.

- **Response times:** `Arrival_Seconds` is measured in seconds, while `Dispatch_Minutes` and `Travel_Minutes` are measured in minutes. Convert measurements when necessary to maintain consistent units.

- **Final reporting week:** September 21, 2026, was provisionally excluded due to possible incomplete reporting. This has not been confirmed as a reporting error.

- **Forecasting evaluation:** Use chronological training and testing periods rather than randomly splitting weekly observations. Both modeling sections will use the same chronological training and testing dates

The cleaned dataset has not been divided into training and testing subsets. The chronological split is performed in 02_train_test_split.qmd before forecasting begins.

# Conclusion

The exploratory analysis found that NYC EMS demand increased during the earlier years of the dataset, experienced a major disruption around 2020, and has remained relatively stable in recent years. Non-life-threatening emergencies generally accounted for more incidents than life-threatening emergencies.

Annual seasonality was weak across the full historical period but more distinguishable during 2022–2026. These differences suggest that historical disruptions and the choice of training period may influence forecasting results.

Overall, the cleaned dataset provides a reliable foundation for forecasting EMS demand and response times. The next stage of the project will evaluate forecasting models and determine how accurately future demand and response times can be predicted.
